UQ Gatton trials cancer drug that could cure dogs with terminal tumours Date: Mon Feb 9 01:00:00 2026 UTC UQ Gatton Professor Rachel Allavena said the drug Enzistat developed by American pharmaceutical company Avammune has the potential to treat cancers in dogs and humans. "It gives dogs in southeast Queensland another option, and it's always nice to do cutting edge trials," she said. "The early data that the company has is that it's helped dogs survive longer and have less bad side effects from their cancer. "We're quite hopeful that for dogs that might not have a lot of options that it might be a useful drug in the future." UQ is looking for 30 dogs with inoperable tumours and 30 dogs in palliative care to be part of the trial. Professor Allavena said they hope the drug can shrink inoperable tumours so they could be removed surgically and give a final hope for dogs in palliative care. "They don't have hope for a cure any other way, but their owners just want to see if they can keep them to be around a little longer and see if it can make them more comfortable," she said. She said a third to a half of dogs will get cancer and it is more common than in lots of other species. Professor Allavena has been researching immune-based cancer therapies for about 15 years and she said it was really hard at times. "It's really hard when we hear about one of our patients passing away," she said. "We do also get a lot of joy from giving people hope or giving the animals options." Anyone interested in joining the trial need a cancer diagnosis and referral from their vet. People involved in the trial would need to give a tablet to their dog twice a day for six weeks and need to come to UQ Gatton three times throughout the trial. The medication and any additional blood tests, biopsies, or examinations are provided as part of the study and owners have to cover any other veterinary costs. Contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au to join the trial. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Of course the ChatGPT dog cancer vaccine spawned a startup (https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/978671/ai-cured-dog-cancer-mrna-vaccine-startup-gamgee) 【turn1042news25】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 2 months ago; Paul Conyngham, an Australian tech entrepreneur, has launched a startup named Gamgee that aims to develop personalized mRNA cancer vaccines for dogs, inspired by his own dog Rosie’s battle with cancer. He claims to have used AI tools like ChatGPT and computational genomics to craft a vaccine that led to shrinkage in Rosie's tumors. Though Gamgee focuses on pet care, its broader ambition extends to personalized treatment for various species, including humans. Rosie’s case, which features prominently in Gamgee’s marketing, has drawn skepticism from experts who question the scientific validity of the claims, noting that Rosie received multiple treatments, making it unclear if the mRNA vaccine caused her improvement. Despite scientific uncertainties, Gamgee has received backing from Y Combinator and is preparing for clinical trials in Australia, with global recruitment underway. The company promises a simple, quick process for veterinarians and highlights promising initial results, though based on a single case. Gamgee is collaborating with Australian universities and aims to scale its personalized medicine approach, although its foundation rests on unverified anecdotal outcomes. Several of her tumours shrank." Conyngham, who stresses on Gamgee's website that he is "not a biologist," credits that intervention with adding years to Rosie's life. Gamgee's stated mission is to do that at scale. In case the canine element is lost on its visitors, the website features a slideshow of adorable dogs alongside ages and purported cancer diagnosis to remind them "who we're building this for." But as I reported for The Verge earlier this year, the science behind Rosie's story is considerably messier than Conyngham's neat account suggests. The exact role AI played in the endeavor wasn't clear, and researchers said the broad claims gave the technology too much credit while minimizing the role of the humans involved. Moreover, the protocol Rosie followed made it impossible to say whether the mRNA vaccine was responsible for her improvement, since it was administered alongside another therapy. That hasn't stopped the idea from attracting support. The startup is backed by storied tech incubator Y Combinator and says it is recruiting for its first clinical trials in Australia, with a waitlist open everywhere else (though Conyngham says they're "accepting cases globally."). On a section on its website aimed at veterinarians, Gamgee touts a roughly 75 percent tumor reduction in its "first documented case," while promising to require less than 20 minutes of a veterinarian's time, no new clinical workflows, and a finished "vaccine in hand" in around four weeks. The company cautions that this timeline is based on a single case and may vary. Costs aren't disclosed on the site. Gamgee says it's working in collaboration with the University of Queensland and institutes at the University of New South Wales in Australia, and Conyngham encourages potential funders or study partners to reach out. Ultimately, the company says its mission extends beyond dogs and other animals to personalized treatments for humans. For a startup built around a single dog whose improvement cannot be clearly attributed to the treatment at the core of its pitch, that's a grand ambition. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Cats could help scientists better understand human cancer, study says (https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/2026/05/30/scientists-find-cancer-gene-similarities-cats-humans-study-says/) 【turn1042news26】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 4 months ago; A recent study led by Louise van der Weyden and international researchers has discovered significant genetic similarities between feline and human cancers, offering promising avenues for shared treatment advancements. Analyzing tumor samples from nearly 500 domestic cats across multiple countries, the researchers identified common mutations in about 1,000 cat genes that correspond to human cancer genes. Among the most striking parallels was the FBXW7 gene, a tumor suppressor found mutated in both feline mammary tumors and human breast cancer, associated with poor prognoses. Published in the journal Science, the research underlines cats as effective disease models due to their genetic closeness to humans and shared living environments that expose them to similar carcinogens. The study also revealed chemotherapy drug vincristine’s effectiveness in treating feline mammary tumors, providing a potential pathway for clinical trials and the development of targeted treatments. While experts like Jaime Modiano stress that more research is needed, the findings mark a significant step toward dual-species cancer therapy, benefiting both feline and human patients. Cancer progresses faster in dogs than in people, meaning researchers can receive quicker results with potential treatments in clinical trials with canines. The bone cancer osteosarcoma is more common in dogs than people, so scientists have learned techniques from the animals on how to treat people with the same cancer, and vice versa. A decade ago, researchers told The Washington Post that dogs were observed more than cats in oncology studies because less was known about feline tumors and cats tended to become more stressed interacting with people. For their study, van der Weyden and other researchers collected tissue samples from domestic cats from Austria, Canada, England, Germany, New Zealand and Scotland. They screened about 1,000 cat genes that are equivalent to human genes associated with cancer. Van der Weyden said she worried they might not find similarities between cat and human cancers, partly because few cat genetic studies had been completed. However, in addition to the gene associated with breast cancer in both species, researchers said they found similarities in human and cat cancers affecting their blood, bones, lungs, skin, gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system. "I was first of all doing it for the cat," said van der Weyden, senior staff scientist at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, a genomics research center in Cambridgeshire, England. "But then to find that there are similarities and we can help humans, that's fantastic." Researchers found that the chemotherapy drug vincristine was effective against cats' mammary tumors, according to the study, which was published in February. They said that finding could guide veterinary pharmaceutical companies in developing treatment for mammary cancer, which is the third-most-common feline cancer and is typically deadly, according to Cornell University's Feline Health Center. "Before we just didn't know; we didn't know what drug you could potentially pick," said Wood, who teaches pathology at the University of Guelph in Ontario. "And now there's sort of a list, at least, that could then proceed to clinical trials." Jaime Modiano, a professor at the University of Minnesota's school of veterinary medicine who was not involved in the research, said the study is a foundation for scientists to learn more about cat and human cancers. However, he said, much more research is required to determine whether the findings can lead to treatments for cats - let alone helping with human cancers. "It's the first step," Modiano said, "in the journey of a thousand miles." -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rescue dog Rosie's cancer shrinks after world-first mRNA vaccine (https://www.theaustralian.com.au/business/technology/tech-boss-uses-ai-and-chatgpt-to-create-cancer-vaccine-for-his-dying-dog/news-story/292a21bcbe93efa17810bfcfcdfadbf7) 【turn1042news27】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 7 months ago; In a groundbreaking medical development, Sydney tech entrepreneur Paul Conyngham used artificial intelligence and mRNA technology to create a customized cancer vaccine for his rescue dog, Rosie. Diagnosed in 2024 with an aggressive mast cell tumor, traditional chemotherapy and surgery failed to stop the cancer. Determined to save her, Conyngham used ChatGPT and AI data processing to analyze Rosie's genomic data, identify cancer mutations, and design a personalized mRNA vaccine with help from experts at the University of NSW. Developed in collaboration with the UNSW RNA Institute and administered by veterinary researchers at the University of Queensland, the vaccine significantly shrank one of Rosie's large tumors. This marks the first known case of a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine being developed for a dog. The success has inspired optimism among oncologists working on similar treatments for humans, highlighting the potential of citizen-led science and AI applications in medicine. Rosie's improved health underscores the promise of mRNA technology in personalized cancer care, both for animals and potentially humans. Mr. Conyngham is now working on developing a second vaccine to target remaining tumors. Rescue dog Rosie’s cancer shrinks after world-first mRNA vaccine Date: Fri Mar 13 09:30:00 2026 UTC Now the hi-tech teamwork has unleashed an experimental medicine that offers hope to human patients, by using mRNA vaccines in oncology. Abandoned in bushland, eight-year-old Rosie found her forever home with Sydney tech entrepreneur Paul Conyngham, who adopted the staffy-shar pei cross from an animal shelter in 2019 - just in time for pandemic lockdowns. Heartbroken when his fur-baby was diagnosed with a deadly mast cell cancer in 2024, Mr ­Conyngham threw thousands of dollars at veterinary chemotherapy and surgery, which slowed but failed to shrink the tumours. Now, after treatment with a custom mRNA cancer vaccine over the Christmas break, the tennis ball-sized tumour on Rosie's hock has shrunk in half, in a recovery that has astounded researchers at the cutting-edge of human cancer treatments. "It was like holy crap, it worked!'' says Martin Smith, an associate professor of computational biology and director of the Ramaciotti Centre for Genomics at the University of NSW. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- A new cancer treatment for cats could help humans, too (https://www.sfchronicle.com/health/article/human-cat-oral-cancer-treatment-20881627.php) 【turn1042news28】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 1.1 years ago; A new study, published by researchers from UCSF, UC Davis, and the University of Pittsburgh, presents a groundbreaking cancer treatment for cats that may also benefit human patients with head and neck tumors. The therapy targets STAT3, a transcription factor known to be hyperactivated in about 75% of human tumors. Researchers created a DNA-based decoy molecule that inhibits STAT3 by mimicking the genetic sequences it typically binds to, thereby preventing it from triggering cancer-promoting genes. In a clinical trial involving 20 pet cats with oral cancer, 35% showed tumor shrinkage or stability, with minimal side effects. One cat, Jak, significantly outlived his prognosis, benefiting from the therapy. The decoy treatment was administered intravenously, an improvement over previous versions requiring direct tumor injection. The findings revealed immune system changes in treated cats, offering potential biomarkers for identifying patients—both feline and human—who may benefit most. With promising results and improved survival rates in responsive cats, researchers are aiming to fund early-phase human trials while continuing feline studies, suggesting possible future cross-species cancer therapies. A new cancer treatment for cats could help humans, too Date: Thu Aug 28 15:00:17 2025 UTC In a study published Thursday, scientists from UCSF, UC Davis and the University of Pittsburgh describe a promising, first of its kind treatment in pet cats with oral cancer. The authors say the approach could benefit people with head and neck tumors, too. "There are common features of cancer in cats and cancer in humans," said author Jennifer Grandis, a professor in UCSF's Department of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery. "We can learn from each other." The new treatment targets the STAT3 transcription factor, a protein that binds specific DNA sequences to affect gene expression. "This transcription factor is hyperactivated in almost three-quarters of human tumors," said author Daniel Johnson, a professor in UCSF's Department of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery. Until now, the protein has proven "incredibly difficult to inhibit," Johnson said. Diese Krebsform gilt beim Menschen wie bei Tieren als besonders aggressiv und schwer behandelbar. Das getestete Medikament zielt auf den Transkriptionsfaktor STAT3, der das Tumorwachstum fördert. Bei 35 % der 20 teilnehmenden Katzen zeigte sich ein positives Ansprechen auf die Therapie mit minimalen Nebenwirkungen. Die Behandlung führte zu teilweiser Besserung oder stabiler Erkrankung, mit einer durchschnittlichen Überlebenszeit von 161 Tagen bei betroffenen Katzen. Die Studie unterstreicht das Potenzial, klinische Studien an Haustieren durchzuführen, da deren Tumore ähnliche Eigenschaften wie menschliche Tumore aufweisen. Zusätzlich konnte eine verstärkte Immunantwort durch erhöhtes PD-1 beobachtet werden, was Ansatzpunkte für eine Kombination mit Checkpoint-Inhibitoren bietet. Der Ansatz zeigt, dass Haustiere vielversprechendere Modelle als Labormäuse sein könnten. Die Studienautoren planen bereits weitere klinische Tests – sowohl für Tiere als auch für Menschen. Die Forschung eröffnet damit neue Wege für eine effektivere und gleichzeitig tierfreundlichere Krebstherapie. Katzen, die in der Krebsforschung oft wenig Beachtung finden, könnten davon stark profitieren. Die Idee, das HNSCC-Medikament an Hauskatzen zu testen, kam der Erstautorin Jennifer Grandis in einem Gespräch mit ihrer Schwester, einer Tierärztin. „Es gibt eine bemerkenswerte klinische, histopathologische und immunologische Ähnlichkeit zwischen HNSCC bei Katzen und Menschen", berichtet die Krebsmedizinerin jetzt mit ihren Kollegen in „Cell Cancer". Zu den Katzen, die von der ersten klinischen Studie profitierten, zählte ein neunjähriger schwarzer Kater namens Jakiro, oder einfach „Jak". Als bei ihm ein HNSCC diagnostiziert wurde, erklärte der Tierarzt seinen Haltern, ihr Liebling hätte nur noch sechs bis acht Wochen zu leben. Es sei wie ein Schlag in die Magengrube gewesen, erinnert sich Tina Thomas, die Besitzerin. „Wir wollten mehr Zeit mit ihm verbringen. Als ich von dieser klinischen Studie erfuhr, wusste ich, dass ich ihn daran teilhaben lassen wollte." Mehrere Monate statt nur Wochen Jak wurde einen Monat lang wöchentlich behandelt; sechs Dosen waren es insgesamt, die man allen vierbeinigen Probanden intravenös spritzte.
